source.title_on_document: Generative Al as a Collaborative Screenwriting Tool Measuring Creative Output Quality VS. Human-Authored Scripts

supplement.where: The text refers to 'Appendix A' for the prompt templates (PDF p. 3, Section II.B). No appendix is in this PDF and no URL is given.
supplement.holds: Standardized prompt templates. The text does not say that the appendix holds any statistics.

paper_design_summary: The authors produced short screenplay scenes on matched premises in four genres under three conditions: written by professional screenwriters (human-only), generated in one pass by a GPT-series model (AI-minimal), and generated by the model and then refined over up to five rounds of feedback from a human editor (iterative human-AI). Industry professionals scored the anonymized scripts blind on a modified script-coverage rubric (narrative coherence, character depth, dialogue authenticity, thematic complexity, emotional resonance), and the conditions were compared with one-way ANOVA. No person was randomly assigned to AI help, and the paper gives no count of scripts, writers, editors, or evaluators.

studies.label: Screenplay corpus under three authorship conditions, blind expert rubric scoring

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-series large language models via a cloud-based inference engine (no specific model named)
ai_tool.how_used: AI-minimal: single-pass generation of the full script from a prompt with minimal edits. Iterative: the model writes a draft and then rewrites it after each round of written critique from a human editor (up to five rounds). Prompts were standardized templates run by Python scripts.

task.description: Short film scripts, one scene per premise, on matched premises in four genres (drama, thriller, comedy, sci-fi).
task.duration: Table 5 (labelled 'hypothetical LLM backend') lists human effort per script: 120 min human-only, 5 min AI-minimal, 25 min iterative human-AI; the conclusion calls the effort metrics hypothetical.

company_involvement.description: No AI company role is described. Both authors list company affiliations (Zero Density Inc; CapitalOne Bank), neither an AI developer.

eligibility.reason: The paper compares script corpora produced under three authorship conditions in what it calls a 'controlled simulation environment'; it describes no random assignment of people to AI help, and its main contrast is AI-generated scripts versus human-written scripts. It gives no count of writers, editors, evaluators, or scripts, so criterion 2 cannot be checked. Outcomes are blind expert ratings of the scripts, so criterion 3 is met. The iterative human-AI arm involves a human editor working with the model, but who that editor was and how many there were is not stated.

one_line_finding: In blind expert rubric scoring, single-pass GPT scripts scored lower than professional human scripts overall (6.26 vs 8.42), while scripts refined over up to five rounds of human-editor feedback scored 8.20 (PDF p. 4, Table 1); no counts, SDs, or test statistics are printed.
open_questions: The paper never states how many scripts, premises, screenwriters, editors, or evaluators there were; only 'the same numbers of screenplays per condition' and a 'moderate sample size of evaluators'.

The study is described as a 'simulation' in a 'virtual setting', Table 5 is labelled 'hypothetical LLM backend', and the conclusion mentions the 'hypothetical nature of effort metrics'. It is unclear whether the rubric scores in Tables 1-4 come from real expert ratings of real scripts.

Table 1 column headers cite references [13] and [14] for the Human-only and AI-minimal columns, and Table 2 cites [15] and [16]; reference [14] is a video-grounding paper. It is unclear whether any of these numbers were taken from other papers.

The 'Significance' column in Table 1 seems to report the three-condition ANOVA; no pairwise post-hoc results are printed, so the iterative vs human-only and iterative vs AI-minimal contrasts have no test.

Should an iterative human-AI condition with an unspecified human editor (no assignment of people) be treated as ai_vs_human context or as a non-random comparison of people (quasi_people/observational)?
notes: Internal inconsistencies in the document: Eq. 4 defines four rubric domains (with 'Thematic Complexity and Emotional Resonance' as one), while Table 1 reports five metrics; the text refers to 'Table IV' and 'Table 4' for the efficiency comparison that appears as Table 5; Figure 5 has two different captions; the text mentions an unexplained 'SAFL framework' (PDF p. 5). Appendix A (prompt templates) is referenced but not included. Question is coded 'none' for all outcomes because no person was assigned to AI assistance; the iterative vs human-only contrast is recorded as comparison_type 'other'.
